summary: Lunar south-pole mission planning demands more than viable coordinates. Low-angle sunlight, terrain-obstructed horizons, and time-dependent Earth visibility create competing constraints on solar power and communications, while launch delays can alter a landing site's suitability. Developed by Team BlackRay, Kaguya integrates NASA lunar elevation models, JPL ephemeris data, and interactive 3D visualization into a unified landing-site analysis platform. Using LRO LOLA and SLDEM2015 terrain data alongside NASA/JPL SPICE-based celestial geometry, Kaguya computes local elevation, slope, terrain horizons, Sun/Earth azimuth and elevation, illumination intervals, and potential direct-to-Earth visibility windows. Its navigable lunar atlas connects orbital exploration with ground-level terrain perspectives, while mission-planning tools quantify sunlight duration, visibility overlap, shadow periods, and the consequences of launch delays. Side-by-side comparisons expose operational trade-offs across landing sites and dates. Crucially, Kaguya preserves terrain-model provenance rather than mixing elevation sources, flags sensitivity to provisional DEMs, and distinguishes geometric visibility from validated solar-power or radio-frequency link budgets. By combining scientific traceability, quantitative scenario analysis, and accessible geographic exploration, Kaguya transforms lunar mission planning from fragmented calculations into an intuitive, evidence-driven decision-support experience.
details:
Kaguya | Interactive Lunar Atlas & Landing Site Navigator

The Challenge

The lunar south pole is among the most scientifically compelling and operationally challenging regions of the Moon. Its rugged topography, deep craters, and extreme illumination conditions make landing-site selection far more complicated than identifying a suitable coordinate on a map. Low solar elevation angles and terrain obstructions can significantly affect power generation and direct-to-Earth communication opportunities, while launch delays and changing mission requirements introduce further uncertainty.

Although scientific tools exist to evaluate these constraints, navigating complex interfaces and interpreting information across multiple platforms can make comparing landing sites and mission dates unnecessarily difficult.

Our Solution

Developed by Team BlackRay, Kaguya is an interactive lunar atlas and landing-site navigator that combines immersive geographic exploration with time-dependent environmental analysis. Our goal is to make exploring the Moon as intuitive as navigating a terrestrial map, while providing the scientific context necessary for evaluating potential landing sites.

Rather than treating a landing site as an isolated coordinate, Kaguya connects geographic exploration, surface conditions, and mission planning within one cohesive platform.

How It Works

Interactive Lunar Atlas: A fully navigable, high-resolution 3D Moon allows users to rotate the globe freely, zoom into detailed terrain, search for locations, and investigate potential landing sites.

Immersive Surface Exploration: Users can descend from orbit to ground level, exploring lunar landscapes through a Street View-like perspective while examining local horizons and the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth.

Mission Planner: Users can configure landing coordinates, dates, and mission durations to evaluate solar illumination, Earth visibility, and potential operational windows. Interactive timelines illustrate how environmental conditions change over time.

Parallel Comparison and Mission Recovery: Side-by-side scenario comparisons allow users to evaluate alternative landing sites and dates, identify operational trade-offs, and investigate contingency plans when launch delays or changing requirements affect an original mission.

Personalized Exploration: Google Sign-In, bookmarked lunar locations, and saved mission configurations allow users to revisit previous analyses through a unified Saved Items dashboard.

Benefits

Accessibility: Brings geographic exploration and scientific analysis into one intuitive interface.

Efficiency: Simplifies comparisons between landing sites, mission dates, and environmental conditions.

Flexibility: Supports custom coordinates, adjustable mission parameters, and alternative scenarios.

Continuity: Enables users to save locations and mission plans for future exploration.

Development Tools and Technology

Kaguya combines Python-based scientific computation with interactive 3D visualization and web development. Our workflow uses Pycharm, Figma, and GitHub for development, testing, and collaboration.

The platform incorporates a detailed 50 GB lunar model, presenting the technical challenge of rendering extensive geographic detail while maintaining a responsive user experience. Its cloud architecture is designed around Google Cloud Storage for large model files, Cloud Run for scientific processing, and Firebase for authentication and saved user information.

Scientific analysis considers how Sun–Earth geometry, local topography, and mission timing interact. Importantly, geometric visibility does not always guarantee an unobstructed line of sight, and Earth visibility alone does not establish communication-link availability.

Creativity and Innovation

Kaguya's innovation lies not simply in displaying lunar information, but in changing how users interact with it. Traditional mapping tools emphasize geographic location, while scientific analysis tools often emphasize numerical outputs. Kaguya combines both approaches, allowing users to explore a location visually and investigate its operational implications.

By integrating seamless orbit-to-surface navigation, dynamic environmental timelines, comparative mission analysis, and persistent exploration, Kaguya transforms complex lunar information into an interactive experience that connects where a mission could land, when conditions may be favorable, and how alternative decisions compare.

Think Google Maps, but with fewer roads and significantly more craters.

Design Considerations

Scientific Accuracy: Distinguishing geometric visibility from terrain-obstructed visibility and recognizing the limitations of environmental indicators.

Performance: Managing a large 3D lunar model through efficient loading and separation of visualization from scientific computation.

Usability: Making specialized lunar information accessible without sacrificing analytical depth.

Adaptability: Supporting changing mission requirements, custom locations, and comparative planning.

Intended Impact

Kaguya aims to make lunar exploration more accessible to mission planners, researchers, educators, students, and space enthusiasts. By bridging complex scientific analysis with intuitive, human-centered design, the platform supports exploratory landing-site assessment, scientific education, and a deeper understanding of the challenges shaping humanity's next lunar expeditions.

Inspired by Princess Kaguya's journey between Earth and the Moon in The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, our project seeks to bring these two worlds closer together.

Our philosophy is simple: So intuitive, it'll feel like you're back on Earth.

After all, exploring another world should be an adventure, not a struggle with the interface.
